learning_outcomes.text: Knows and understands the importance of physics as a natural science, its place and role in today's science and technology; recognizes the mutual relations between theory and experiment.
Has up-to-date knowledge on the structure of matter and fundamental interactions in nature.

Has knowledge in the field of classical mechanics of a material point and a rigid body, relativistic mechanics, gravity, oscillatory and wave motion, electromagnetic interactions necessary to understand basic physical phenomena in nature and technology, and especially in electrical engineering, electronics and mechanics.
Can use the international SI system, can convert units.
Acquires mathematical foundations for describing physical phenomena, knows examples of applying vector, differential and integral calculus in physics.
Can apply appropriate physical laws and principles to solve problems of dynamics of a material point and a rigid body.
Independently solves problems in the field of classical and relativistic mechanics.
Independently solves problems in electrostatics using the concepts of electric field intensity, electric potential and electrical capacitance.
Recognizes the need to develop the ability to use mathematical tools in the description of physical phenomena.
Understands the paramount role of the laws of physics and acquires the ability to use these laws to explain the course of phenomena in nature.
The student is prepared, based on knowledge of physical principles, to undertake actions aimed at the development of technical sciences, including mechanics and electrical engineering.

syllabus_topics: Practical ability to use vector calculus in physics: Vector in Cartesian coordinate system, operations on vectors in this system; application of scalar and vector product to define basic physical quantities.

Physics as a rigorous natural science: Methods of cognition in physics, experiment, physical quantities, range of physical quantities, SI unit system, laws, theories, microworld – macroworld. Mathematical methods in physics. Solving physics problems: formulating the problem, hypotheses, choosing solution methods, correspondence principle.
Kinematics of a material point in a vector approach: One-dimensional motion and motion in a plane. Uniformly accelerated motion, free fall, projectile motion. Circular motion, curvilinear motion.

Kinematics of a material point: Practical ability to calculate instantaneous velocity and instantaneous acceleration. Analysis of circular motion and curvilinear motion (projectile motion), normal, tangential and total acceleration. Finding the trajectory of curvilinear motion. Relationship between linear and angular quantities using the example of velocity and acceleration.

Dynamics of a material point: Fundamental interactions. Laws of dynamics in translational and rotational motion. Momentum, angular momentum, conservation of momentum, examples. Contact forces and friction. Inertial and non-inertial systems, inertial forces. Gravitational force, motion under the influence of a central force, Kepler's laws, gravitational field, force fields.

Dynamics of a material point: Practical ability to use the laws of dynamics: procedure for solving dynamic problems, finding the resultant force and acceleration of a body. Discussion of examples where fictitious forces are introduced. Motion of a body in a uniform gravitational field. Solving problems using the principle of conservation of momentum.
Work and energy: Work of constant and variable force. Energy, kinetic energy, conservative and non-conservative forces, potential energy. Conservation of mechanical energy and total energy.

Galilean and Lorentz transformation: Basics of special and general relativity. Simultaneity of events, length contraction, time dilation, velocity addition. Relativistic energy; conservation of mass-energy.

Work and energy: Calculation of work done on a free particle – kinetic energy. Work of a variable force. Examples of conservative forces and fields – potential energy. Practical ability to use the principle of conservation of mechanical energy. Relationship between potential energy and force.
Translational and rotational motion of a rigid body: Torque, moment of inertia, Steiner's theorem, angular momentum, conservation of angular momentum.

Kinematics and dynamics of a rigid body: Practical ability to find the moment of inertia for discrete and continuous mass distributions. Application of the principle of conservation of mechanical energy and the laws of dynamics to rotational motion of a rigid body and rolling without slipping.
Oscillatory motion: Simple harmonic motion, damped oscillatory motion, forced oscillations – resonance, energy of oscillatory motion, superposition of oscillations.

Oscillatory motion: Solution of the simple harmonic oscillator equation, finding natural oscillation frequencies. Calculation of velocity and acceleration in harmonic motion. Analysis of the dependence of quantities describing a harmonic oscillator on time and position. Mathematical and physical pendulums. Dependence of damped oscillator amplitude on time. Analysis of frequency, amplitude and phase for a forced oscillator. Ability to draw and analyze resonance curves. Discussion of resonance conditions. Practical ability to find the results of superposition of arbitrary harmonic oscillations.
Mechanical waves: Simple solutions of the wave equation. Analysis of energy transport in wave motion. Wave interference: standing waves, wave beats, analysis of complex waves, Doppler effect.

Mechanical waves: Mechanism of wave propagation, wave motion equation, simple solutions of the wave equation, energy transport in wave motion, standing waves, wave beats, analysis of complex waves, Doppler effect.
Statics and dynamics of fluids: Pascal's and Archimedes' laws. General description of flow: continuity equation, Bernoulli's law, dynamic lift force.

Electrostatics: Analysis of electric field intensity from charge distribution. Practical ability to use Gauss's law. Relationship between electric potential and electric field intensity. Calculation of capacitance of capacitor systems.
Kinetic theory of gases and thermodynamics: Laws of thermodynamics, internal energy, Carnot cycle.
Electrostatics: Coulomb's law, electric field, Gauss's law, electric potential, electrical capacitance, energy of electric field, dielectrics, dielectric polarization.
Electric current: Current intensity and density, classical theory of conductivity, Ohm's law, resistance, conductance, superconductivity, work and power of current, DC circuits.

Magnetic field: Sources of magnetic field, magnetic induction vector, properties of magnetic field, motion of charges in magnetic field, current-carrying conductor in magnetic field, Hall effect. Magnetic field of current-carrying conductors. Ampere's law, interaction of parallel current-carrying conductors. Biot-Savart law.
Electromagnetic induction: Faraday's law of induction, mutual and self-induction, energy of magnetic field.
Electromagnetic oscillations: LC and RLC circuit, resonance, power in AC circuit.

assessment_methods.method: Participation in a discussion during lectures

assessment_rules: To be admitted to the subject exam, students must have a positive grade (at least 3.0) from the auditorium exercises. The exam will be conducted in three terms (first term and two retake terms). Attendance at auditorium classes is mandatory. Students are required to prepare for exercises as indicated by the instructor (e.g., in the form of problem sets). Student performance evaluation may be based on oral or written statements in the form of a colloquium, which, in accordance with the AGH study regulations, translates into the final grade for this form of classes. For students who attended the exercises and did not receive credit, the instructor is obliged to conduct an additional written verification of the student's knowledge at the last class or at another time to enable them to obtain credit.
